title: Everything Talks to Everything
principle: Keeping things steady like this is called homeostasis.

t: Stand up quickly. Before you notice anything, four different systems have already reacted.
Stand up fast and your blood tries to pool in your legs. Within one heartbeat, sensors, nerves, heart and vessels have all responded — and you noticed none of it.
sub: No decision was taken anywhere. Work out what the arrangement must be for that to happen.

question: How can four systems react before you have even noticed?
How is a response coordinated across systems faster than conscious awareness?
options: A sensor triggers a loop that corrects itself automatically
The brain works it out very quickly
It is a coincidence that they all do the right thing
stages.outcome: A sensor triggers a loop that corrects itself automatically
note: Commit. The mechanism is the same one a thermostat uses, and it needs no intelligence anywhere in it.

t: Build the loop that stops you fainting. Any part fits any slot, so it is on you.
Assemble the baroreflex. Placement is unconstrained; each misassignment fails a specific test.

label: Reports back so it knows when to stop

name: Notice anything at all
Detection
pass: The drop in pressure is detected.
The stimulus is transduced into a signal.
fail: Pressure fell and nothing registered it.
No sensor, no signal. A correction cannot begin.

name: React in time
Speed
pass: The message arrives within a heartbeat.
Neural conduction delivers the signal in well under a second.
fail: It was noticed and the news went nowhere fast enough.
Detected but not conducted: hormonal signalling alone takes seconds to minutes, and you would already be on the floor.

name: Actually fix it
Correction
pass: Heart rate up, vessels tighten, pressure recovers.
Heart rate and vascular tone rise; arterial pressure is restored.
fail: A perfect alarm and nobody acting on it.
Signal without an effector changes nothing. Sensing is not regulating.

name: Know when to stop
Feedback
pass: The correction is fed back, so the response scales down as the error closes.
fail: It overcorrected and kept going. Your pressure swings instead of settling.
Open loop: without feedback the response does not know the error has closed, so it overshoots and oscillates. That is not a small flaw — it is why open-loop control is unusable here.

win: It corrects itself and then settles down. Nobody decided anything.
A closed negative-feedback loop. It regulates without any part of it knowing what blood pressure is for.
lose: Read which test failed — it names the missing job.
Each failure names the element that was absent. Reassign and re-test.

t: Keeping things steady like this is called homeostasis.
Holding conditions steady against disturbance is homeostasis, and it is done with feedback loops rather than decisions.
Homeostasis: regulation by negative feedback. Sensor, comparator, effector, and a return path — the same architecture wherever it appears, and it requires no intelligence at any point.

Cannon named it in 1926, and Bernard's milieu intérieur set it up seventy years earlier. The insight is that an organism does not tolerate its environment — it maintains an internal one, and nearly every physiological variable you can name is defended this way.
sub: Your temperature, water, sugar and salt are all held steady the same way.
Temperature, blood glucose, pH, water, calcium, oxygen — all regulated by loops of this same shape.
The feedback is what makes it stable. Remove it and the response overshoots and oscillates rather than settling.

Which is why homeostatic failure is so often oscillation rather than simple absence: a loop with damaged feedback does not stop working, it starts hunting, and a system that swings is frequently more dangerous than one that has merely stopped.

q: Why does the loop need a signal coming back?
Why is the return path essential rather than a refinement?
Why does open-loop control fail here specifically?
options: So it knows when to stop and does not overshoot
So the brain can keep a record
why: Without something reporting back, the response has no way of knowing the problem is fixed. It keeps pushing, overshoots, and then has to correct the other way.

Feedback is what makes the response proportional to the remaining error. Without it the effector runs at full output regardless, so the system overshoots and oscillates rather than settling — instability, not just imprecision.

The controlled variable is the same one being sensed, which is what closes the loop and makes the correction self-limiting. Open loop, the output is independent of the result, so any disturbance or drift accumulates. Baroreflex failure produces exactly this clinically: pressure that swings wildly rather than pressure that is simply low.

t: Type 1 diabetes is one of these loops with the sensor's answer missing.

Blood glucose is held steady by a loop in which insulin is the effector signal. Destroy the cells that make it and the loop opens: glucose is still sensed and nothing can act on the reading. Treatment is prosthetic feedback — measure, calculate, dose — and closed-loop insulin pumps are an engineer's attempt to rebuild the return path the body lost.
